newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ may need to review signalling methods - Brash.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ may need to review signalling methods - Brash.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash said on Monday there may be a need for the bank to look again at its signalling techniques to the financial markets.

"To date, we seem to be able to convey our view of monetary conditions very effectively through our quarterly inflation forecasts and comments made in conjunction with the publication of these," Brash told Federated Farmers in Invercargill.

"But it is not perfect -- we can easily communicate to the market that we want monetary conditions tighter, or easier, but the present approach is less well suited to telling the market how much tighter, or how much firmer."

Brash said this had not been a major problem to date, but with more and more participation in the New Zealand market of overseas institutions, familiar with a more traditional, directive approach to monetary policy implementation, the potential for confusion and misunderstanding had grown.

Following the release of lower-than-expected September quarter inflation data on October 15, the bank issued a statement saying that while the inflation outcome was good news, 'at this stage any further easing in monetary conditions would be inappropriate'.
At the time, 90 day bill rates were at 9.4 percent and the exchange rate on the Trade-Weighted Index, was at 66.5
"Within a few trading days, the exchange rate had appreciated sharply, with the TWI at almost 68, and 90 day interest rates only a little changed, at 9.3 percent," Brash said.
He said the combination constituted quite a significant firming in overall monetary conditions, and the bank issued a second statement saying that conditions were a little firmer than needed.
"What happened over those few days to swing conditions around from easing too quickly, to being too tight?" Brash asked rhetorically.

"Although there had been no specific mention of interest rates in the first statement, it appears that many in the financial markets interpreted the statement as implying that the bank would be quite unwilling to see 90 day interest rates fall
"With such an apparent commitment to preventing interest rates from falling, the New Zealand dollar seemed a one-way bet, and the exchange rate rose strongly."

Brash said the bank had for some considerable time made it explicit that it fully accepted both interest rates and the exchange rate affected inflation, and that for this reason it could be more or less comfortable with a range of interest rate/exchange rate combinations.
"But it seems that we still have considerable work to do to remind people of that," he said.
"It is certainly important to remember that the bank is looking at both interest rates and the exchange rate in making its assessment of the appropriateness of monetary conditions."
